Small amount of nitrogenous wastes are also eliminated through saliva and tears. 4.9 Excretion in other organisms Different organisms use varied strategies in excretion. Specific excretory organs are absent in unicellular organisms. These organisms remove waste products by simple diffusion from the body surface into the surrounding water. Fresh water organisms like Amoeba, Paramoecium possess osmoregulatory organelle called contractile vacuole. It collects excess water and waste from the cell and slowly moves in the cytoplasm, reaches the surface and bursts to release its content to outside. The main excretion takes place through body surface (Diffusion). Multicellular organisms possess different excretory organs for removal of waste materials from the body. Structural and functional complexity of excretory organs increases from sponges to humans. Excretion91 Sponges and coelenterates do not have special excretory organs. Water transportation occurs in each cell. Excretory organs are first seen in platyhelmenthes. They are called as flame cells. This is true to our body which is a living cellular factory and for other organisms as well while performing various metabolic activities wastes are generated at regular intervals from the bodies of living organisms. When we think about this matter, we get many doubts. Such thought provoking questions will lead to understand excretion process clearly. Let us discuss such kind of questions in this lesson. Living organisms need energy for their survival and to perform metabolic activities. They are either anabolic activities or catabolic activities. These are collectively called as metabolic activities. All the organisms use different substances for metabolic activities. Different products are generated as a result of these metabolic activities. We have already learnt that different kinds of materials are produced out of various metabolic activities. Some of these may be harmful for the organism are removed from their body or packed and stored in some other forms. These are all wastes produced in the body of an organism. We have already discussed how organisms get rid of gaseous wastes generated during photosynthesis or respiration. Other metabolic activities generate nitrogenous wastes that have to be removed along with salts, excess water and several other materials. Excretion is the term coined for all the biological process involved in separation and removal of wastes or non useful products from the body. (In latin ex means 'out', crenere means 'shift'.) Now let us study how excretion takes place in human beings. 4.1 Excretion in Human Beings A number of reactions take place during various metabolic activities. Many useful substances and energy are produced. At the same time many other things happen such as, toxic wastes may be produced, water content may increase, ionic balance (homeostasis) in the body may be disturbed. The waste products include carbon dioxide, water, nitrogenous compounds like ammonia, urea, uric acid, bile pigments, excess salts etc. The most poisonous of all waste products of metabolism is ammonia. x Where are these waste materials produced? x How does the body manage them? x Is there a way to detect their presence in our body? It is situated in the pelvic region on the ventral side of the rectum in the abdomen. It stores 300-800ml of urine temporarily which is brought by two ureters. 4.3.3 Urethra It is a tube that takes urine from urinary bladder to outside. The opening of urinary bladder into urethra is guarded by a ring of muscles or sphincter. Urethra is 4 cm long in females and open in to vestibule where as in males it is about 20cm long. Its opening is separate in females but is in common with the reproductive tract in males (urino-genital duct). 4.4 Micturition The urine is temporarily stored in the bladder. There are two sets of circular sphincter muscles in the bladder. When the bladder is filling up, both these sets of muscles are constricted, so the exit is closed. However as the pressure of the urine increases the walls of the bladder are stretched and this triggers off an automatic reflex action which causes the upper sphincter to relax. But the lower sphincter is under the control of brain. So urination is controlled. Control of urination is not possessed by very young children but is gradually learned. Urinary bladder can store a maximum of 700-800 ml. of urine. Urge for micturition occurs when urinary bladder is filled with 300 - 400 ml. of urine. The stretched bladder stimulates nerve endings and sends signlas to the brain. At this time the urge becomes painful and leads to voluntary micturition (release of urine from urinary bladder). Total amount of urine excreted per day is about 1.6-1.8 litres. Its quantity increases with larger intake of fluids like water, fruit juices and decreases with lesser intake. Excretion87 4.5 Composition of urine Urine is light yellowish fluid. Urochrome formed by the breakdown of haemoglobin in the blood is responsible for the yellowish colour of urine. It is a transparent fluid formed by urinary system. Composition of normal urine varies considerably depending on several factors. For instance taking a protein rich diet will results the formation of more urea in the urine. This is because the proteins get de-aminated in the liver with subsequent formation of urea. Even sugar can appear in a normal person after a heavy intake of carbohydrates (sugars). A large intake of liquids or water - rich food increases the volume of water in the blood, hence more often urine is excreted. Urine contains 96% of water, 2.5% of organic substances (urea, uric acid, creatine, creatinine, water soluble vitamins, hormones, and oxalates etc) and 1.5% of inorganic solutes (sodium, chloride, phosphate, sulphate, magnesium, calcium, iodine etc). It is acidic (pH=6.0)in the beginning but gradually becomes alkaline due to breakdown of urea to form ammonia. x What happens if both kidneys fail completely? parsed_output.answer: Excretion is the process by which the body removes waste materials and excess substances from the body. In humans, the main organ responsible for excretion is the kidney. The process of urine formation involves four main stages: glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption, tubular secretion, and the formation of concentrated urine. The kidneys filter the blood through the nephrons, which are the structural and functional units of the kidney. The nephron consists of the Bowman’s capsule, glomerulus, proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), Henle’s loop, distal convoluted tubule (DCT), and collecting tubule. During glomerular filtration, blood is filtered through the glomerulus, and the filtrate moves into the Bowman’s capsule. In the PCT, useful substances like water, glucose, and ions are reabsorbed back into the blood. In the DCT and Henle’s loop, further reabsorption and secretion of ions occur. The final urine is then collected in the collecting tubule and transported to the urinary bladder for storage and excretion through the urethra.
